title: What is a feature flag: a way to turn features on/off without deploying new code (using tools like LaunchDarkly or simple config): and why is it useful (test in production, gradual rollout, instant rollback)?
shortTitle: What a feature flag is and why it is useful
keyPoints: A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a redeploy, decoupling deployment from release.
Flags enable testing in production by exposing a feature only to internal users or a small percentage while watching real behavior.
Instant rollback is the standout benefit: flipping a flag off disables a feature in seconds with no redeploy or rollback pipeline.
Flag types include release flags (gradual rollout), kill switches (disable under load), experiment flags (A/B tests), and permission flags (user segments).
Flags must be evaluated consistently per user (stable bucketing) and have a safe default so a flag-service outage does not break requests.
Release flags must be removed promptly after full rollout, because unmanaged flags accumulate into technical debt.

s1_definition.oneliner: A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns functionality on or off without a redeploy, decoupling deployment from release so you can test in production, roll out gradually, and roll back instantly.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Feature flag** – A runtime switch (boolean or richer rule) evaluated at request time that decides whether a piece of functionality is active.
- **Decoupling** – The deployed binary contains both code paths; the flag selects which one runs, separating deploying code from releasing a feature.
- **Sources** – Config file, environment variable, database, or a dedicated service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith) for dynamic changes.
- **Types** – Release flag (gradual rollout), kill switch (disable under load), experiment flag (A/B test), permission flag (user segments).
- **Key benefits** – Test in production safely, gradual rollout limiting blast radius, instant rollback by flipping the flag off.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a feature flag at the National Bank of India as a light switch for a new service, wired in advance but kept off. The new instant-transfer feature is already built into the app and shipped to every branch, but the switch is off so customers do not see it. The bank can flip it on just for Rajesh first, then for 10% of customers, then everyone, and if something looks wrong, flip it straight off in seconds with no need to send out a new app.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Feature Flag Lifecycle
======================

  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  1. DEPLOY      │  Code shipped with flag OFF
  │  (flag OFF)     │  Users see nothing new
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  2. INTERNAL    │  Flag ON for internal testers
  │  (beta test)    │  Rajesh, Priya test with real data
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  3. GRADUAL     │  1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%
  │  (rollout)      │  Watch metrics at each step
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  4. FULL        │  Flag ON for 100% of users
  │  (release)      │  Feature fully live
  └────────┬────────┘
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐
  │  5. CLEANUP     │  Remove the flag and old code path
  │  (remove flag)  │  Reduce technical debt
  └─────────────────┘

  At ANY step: flip flag OFF -> instant rollback (2 seconds)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that decides whether functionality is active, allowing you to turn a feature on or off without deploying new code. The flag value is read at request time from a source that can change without a redeploy, and because the deployed binary already contains both code paths, flipping the flag just selects which one runs. This decouples deploying code from releasing a feature.

The three key benefits are: testing in production safely by enabling a feature only for internal users or a small percentage, gradual rollout by increasing exposure step by step while watching metrics, and instant rollback by flipping the flag off in seconds without any redeploy. Flags also enable trunk-based development since unfinished work can be merged behind a flag that is off. At the National Bank of India, the instant-transfer feature shipped dark, was enabled first for internal testers like Rajesh, then for 10% of customers with stable per-user bucketing, then widened to everyone, and when an incident occurred, flipping the kill switch disabled it instantly.

Remember one sentence: feature flags decouple deployment from release, giving you instant rollback, gradual rollout, and safe production testing, but remove release flags promptly to avoid technical debt.
